nameStory: This tiny mite's scientific name hints at its close relationship with spirea plants - 'paraspiraeae' means 'near spirea.' Like many gall mites, it doesn't have a widely-used common name because it's so small and specialized that most people never notice it, even when it's creating its distinctive plant growths right under our noses.
description: Eriophyes paraspiraeae is a microscopic gall mite that's far too small to see without magnification - typically less than 0.2mm long. These cream-colored, worm-like creatures have only two pairs of legs (unlike most mites which have four pairs) and elongated, carrot-shaped bodies. You'll never spot the mite itself, but you'll definitely notice the abnormal growths or 'galls' it creates on spirea and related plants. These mites are actually arachnids, more closely related to spiders than to insects.

idTips.label: Plant Galls
idTips.description: Look for unusual bumps, blisters, or fuzzy growths on spirea leaves and stems - these felt-like or warty galls house the mites and are your main clue to their presence

idTips.label: Host Plants
idTips.description: Found exclusively on spirea and closely related plants in the rose family - if you're not looking at spirea, you're not looking at this mite

idTips.label: Gall Texture
idTips.description: The galls feel slightly fuzzy or velvety to the touch, often with a greenish or reddish tint that stands out against normal leaf tissue

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: The mites themselves are invisible to the naked eye, but their galls range from pinhead-sized to pea-sized depending on the infestation

idTips.label: Distribution
idTips.description: Galls typically cluster on young growth, leaf undersides, or along leaf veins where the tender plant tissue is easiest for mites to manipulate

habitat: Found in gardens, parks, and naturalized areas throughout New England wherever spirea shrubs grow, from sea level to mid-elevations. This species particularly favors ornamental spireas in landscaped areas, though it can also occur on wild spirea species in woodland edges and old fields. Look for them in both sunny and partially shaded locations where their host plants thrive.

seasonality.spring: Mites become active as spirea leaves emerge, beginning to form new galls on fresh growth. Early galls appear as small, pale bumps on young leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak gall development occurs now - look for fully-formed, fuzzy growths that are most obvious and numerous. This is the best time to spot their handiwork.
seasonality.fall: Galls begin to brown and harden as mites prepare for winter. Some galls may split open, releasing mites to find overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Mites overwinter hidden in bark crevices and bud scales. Old galls remain visible as brown, dried bumps on bare branches.

funFact: These microscopic mites are essentially plant magicians - they inject chemicals that completely reprogram the plant's growth, forcing it to build them custom homes (galls) complete with nutritious inner walls that the mites eat like living in an edible house!
confusionNotes: The galls might be confused with plant diseases, insect damage, or other types of mite galls, but the specific fuzzy texture and exclusive association with spirea plants helps narrow it down. Remember: if it's not on spirea, it's not this species.
contextualKnowledge: Many gardeners mistakenly think galls are caused by diseases or harmful insects and try to spray them away, but these mites are generally harmless to plant health and are actually fascinating examples of how tiny creatures can manipulate much larger organisms.
compareHints: Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite which creates smooth, nail-like projections, or the Lime Felt Gall Mite which makes dense, hair-like patches, this species creates more irregularly-shaped, moderately fuzzy galls. The host plant is your best clue - each Eriophyes species is extremely loyal to its particular plant family, so spirea galls mean you've found paraspiraeae.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates elongated, finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that forms reddish blisters on fruit trees, the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite creates distinctly rounded, bump-like galls.

Red Nail Gall Mites create the most dramatically shaped galls in their genus - while relatives like the Lime Felt Gall Mite create fuzzy patches and others make simple bumps or blisters, only tiliae produces these unmistakable nail or horn-shaped protrusions.
Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates short, nail-like bumps on linden trees, the Plum Finger Gall Mite makes much longer, more cylindrical projections.

While many Eriophyes species create galls on different trees, the Alder Leaf Gall Mite's small, simple dome-shaped galls are quite different from relatives like the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that causes broad, blistered areas rather than distinct bumps.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-shaped galls on linden trees or finger-like projections on cherry leaves, the Birch Leaf Gall Mite creates relatively simple bumps and fuzzy patches.
Eriophyes rhoinus differs from its relatives primarily by its host plant preference for sumac species, while other Eriophyes mites specialize on different trees like cherry, maple, or alder.

While many Eriophyes mites in New England create galls on different trees, the Lime Felt Gall Mite is unique in producing that characteristic felt texture - its close relative the Red Nail Gall Mite makes hard, nail-like projections on linden leaves, while others like the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite create smooth pouches.
Unlike other Eriophyes species that target maples, cherries, or birches, this species is exclusively found on viburnums.
Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite that creates elongated finger-like projections, the Maple Gall Mite produces rounder, more dome-shaped galls.

Eriophyes leionotus differs from its relatives primarily by its specific host plant preferences and gall characteristics rather than the mite's appearance, since all Eriophyes species look remarkably similar under magnification.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-like projections (Red Nail Gall Mite) or finger-shaped growths (Plum Finger Gall Mite), the Serviceberry Gall Mite creates more subtle, pouch-like swellings.

Unlike other Eriophyes mites that create finger-like projections (like Plum Finger Gall Mite) or felt-like patches (like Lime Felt Gall Mite), the Pearleaf Blister Mite creates smooth, dome-shaped blisters.

Unlike its relatives that create felt-like patches (Lime Felt Gall Mite) or target fruit trees (Pearleaf Blister Mite), the lime gall mite creates distinct raised bumps specifically on basswood leaves.
